description: How websites work: servers, clients, standards

screens.body: A website isn't magic — it's just files. Text, images, and code sitting on a computer somewhere. When you visit a site, your browser downloads those files and draws the page for you. The computer that stores and sends the files is called a server.

options: Files on a server, drawn by your browser
A program installed on your phone
check.question: A website is really…

screens.heading: A website is just files
screens.keyPoint: Websites are files on a server, drawn by your browser.

screens.body: The client is your side: the browser on your laptop or phone. It asks for pages. The server is the other side: a computer that's always on, holding the site's files. It answers requests. Every visit is the same loop: the client asks, the server answers.
screens.heading: The client asks, the server answers
screens.keyPoint: Client asks, server answers — that's every web visit.

screens.body: Front-end development is everything the user sees and touches — the layout, buttons, and pages running in the browser. Back-end development is everything behind the scenes — the data, accounts, and rules living on the server. This course is mostly front-end: you'll build what people see.

options: What the user sees and touches in the browser
check.question: Front-end development is…

screens.heading: Front-end vs back-end
screens.keyPoint: Front-end is what users see; back-end is the hidden machinery.

screens.body: Web pages are built from three languages, each with one job. HTML is markup — it structures the content (headings, paragraphs, buttons). CSS is style rules — it controls how things look (colors, sizes, layout). JavaScript is scripting — it makes the page respond (clicks, typing, updates). Think of a house: HTML is the frame, CSS is the paint, JavaScript is the electricity.

options: HTML structures, CSS styles, JavaScript adds behavior
CSS structures, HTML styles, JavaScript hosts sites
All three do the same job
check.question: Which language does what?

screens.heading: Three languages, three jobs
screens.keyPoint: HTML structures, CSS styles, JavaScript behaves.

screens.body: The web works because everyone follows the same rules. The W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) sets the standards for HTML and CSS, so every browser reads the same code the same way. When your code follows the standards, it works everywhere — that's why validators exist, to check your work against the rules.

options: So every browser reads the same code the same way
check.question: Web standards matter…

screens.heading: Standards keep the web working
screens.keyPoint: Standards mean your code works in every browser.

screens.body: Here's the full trip: you type a URL, and the browser looks up which server owns that address. It sends a request — 'give me this page.' The server finds the files and sends them back as a response. Your browser then builds the page on your screen. All of this happens in a blink.

options: The browser finds the server's address
check.question: What happens FIRST when you visit a site?

screens.heading: How a page gets to you
screens.keyPoint: Look up the server, request the files, build the page.

screens.body: Everything in this course builds on this picture. You'll write the files (HTML), style them (CSS), make them respond (JavaScript), and finally publish them to a real server so anyone can visit. By the end, you'll have put a real site on the real internet.

options: Build, style, and publish real web pages
Only read about how websites work
check.question: In this course you will…

screens.heading: Now you build it
screens.keyPoint: You'll go from files on your laptop to a live site.
